verdicts.trueWording: Literary agents, publishers, fan letters, other authors
verdicts.note: Content Description: correspondence series arranged in ten categories, that string among them; repository is University of Oregon Libraries SCUA, Coll 270. Page carries no container/item list and no correspondent names: 'Detailed Description of the Collection' is only a link to the UO guide, and Names and Subjects lists subject terms only. Whole page text is 11.4KB, read in full. Page says 'categories' where the claim says 'subseries'.

verdicts.trueWording: Gene Wolfe and Ursula Le Guin were friends.
verdicts.note: First sentence of the post body, verbatim; byline 'Posted by noisms'. Next parenthesis on the same line gives the evidence: Wolfe talks about it in the interview linked the previous day. No Le Guin statement is cited anywhere in the post. Live blogspot page fetched raw.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that this interview is offered as evidence of the Wolfe-Le Guin friendship - the 15 April post never mentions Le Guin
verdicts.trueWording: This is a nice interview with him
verdicts.note: Quotation verbatim in the post body. 'Video' limb holds: the post embeds youtube.com/embed/0Pf-DyEEGlU and says he warms up 'after the first 10 minutes'. The friendship framing is supplied only by the companion 16 April post (index 727), which cites 'the interview I linked to yesterday'; on its own this page is a death notice with no Le Guin mention. Repair by citing both posts.

verdicts.trueWording: Wolfe is so good he leaves me speechless
verdicts.note: Open Library search-inside page fetched raw (the cited URL): 4 hits, each snippet reading the quoted sentence followed by 'says Ursula Le Guin' (one hit renders it '- Ursula Le Guin'). Books are David Pringle's 'Science fiction: the 100 best novels' (2 editions) and 'The ultimate guide to science fiction' (2 editions). Evidence is full-text-search snippets of the scanned books, not the book page, which is behind Archive.org lending.

verdicts.trueWording: and it has drawn numerous peer tributes
verdicts.note: Verbatim on the cited search-inside page (2 hits, both Pringle's 100 Best Novels), in context '...intelligent novel, supremely well written- and it has drawn numerous peer tributes:'. The Budrys limb, invisible in the cited page's truncation, was recovered by a second Open Library search-inside on the same book: the snippet runs 'says Ursula Le Guin; simply overwhelm-ing adds Algis Budrys.' So Le Guin's sentence is indeed printed beside Budrys's.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the contrast with the Melville line on the jackets - the cited page says nothing about jackets, Melville, or publication decades
verdicts.trueWording: four hits, two Pringle titles, all the speechless sentence
verdicts.note: Cited page supports the first half exactly: 'About 4 results', across 'Science fiction: the 100 best novels' (2 editions) and 'The ultimate guide to science fiction' (2 editions), every snippet the speechless sentence. Neither the 1980s/1990s dating nor the jacket comparison appears there. Independent check on the same host does confirm the other blurb exists: an Open Library search-inside for 'Wolfe is our Melville' returns 9 hits, several visibly Tor jacket copy attributed to Ursula K. Le Guin. Repair by adding that second citation.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that no corpus-linguistic study is indexed - only the word 'stylometry' was queried
verdicts.note: Live Scholar results page fetched raw, no captcha: 'Your search - "Gene Wolfe" stylometry - did not match any articles.' So the zero-result limb is verbatim. The wider limb is an inference from one query string: a second Scholar query, "Gene Wolfe" "corpus linguistics", returns '5 results', headed by the Nichols/Lynn/Purzycki 2014 paper. None of those five is a study of Wolfe's prose (they mention him in passing), so the claim's spirit survives, but the cited page cannot carry the 'corpus-linguistic' half.

verdicts.trueWording: meta.count 3; no result names Gene Wolfe
verdicts.note: OpenAlex API fetched raw; claim carries no quotation, hence substance. meta.count = 3. Titles: an information-theoretic clustering of Shakespearean-era authorship (Arefin/Craig/Moscato 2014); 'Megalite: A New Spanish Literature Corpus for NLP Tasks' (2021); 'Representing the Digital Humanities Community' network visualization (2015). None concerns Gene Wolfe.

verdicts.trueWording: Clark Howard and Gene Wolfe, multiple-award winning writers in mystery
verdicts.note: Both limbs fail against the author-hosted PDF (fetched, 793KB, text extracted with pdftotext, 8,671 words). 'Wolfe' occurs four times, and the paper's discussion section states that Clark Howard and Gene Wolfe each have five stories in their respective genres in the full dataset but only one in the reduced dataset - so Gene Wolfe IS in the corpus. Two other hits are Gary K. Wolfe, Critical Terms for Science Fiction (text and bibliography). Google Scholar's snippet for the paper independently shows the same Gene Wolfe sentence.

verdicts.trueWording: the paucity of detailed analyses available
verdicts.note: Cambridge Core Preface page fetched raw; phrase appears verbatim in the Preface text shown on the page, by-lined Peter Wright, Attending Daedalus pp. xi-xii, Liverpool University Press 2003, in the sentence beginning 'Confronted, then, with the magnitude and range of Wolfe's output...'. The phrase sits mid-Preface rather than in its first sentence, and the Preface itself opens the book.
